questions.q: According to the lesson, what is the single most common reason governance programs fail?
options: Scope that tries to cover all enterprise data at once instead of a phased, named scope
Choosing the wrong database vendor
Having too many stewards
Writing the charter in business language instead of technical language
questions.explain: A charter with no boundaries gives the program no way to ever declare success or prioritize work — the lesson's central scope warning.

questions.q: In a correctly built RACI matrix, how many people should be marked Accountable for a given activity?
options: Exactly one
As many as possible, for full collaboration
Zero — accountability should be implicit
Exactly the same number as Responsible
questions.explain: The lesson's core discipline: every row needs exactly one Accountable, never zero and never more than one.

questions.q: What size does the lesson suggest for a working council's voting membership?
options: Roughly six to ten members
At least fifty members for full representation
Exactly two members
As many as possible to be fully inclusive
questions.explain: The lesson describes six to ten voting members as large enough for range but small enough to actually reach decisions.

questions.q: What is the problem with identifying stakeholders informally, by who shows up to meetings?
options: It tends to miss people whose objections surface later, after a policy is already written — the most expensive time to find out
It identifies too many stakeholders and wastes time
It only works for very small organizations
It is required by regulation to use a formal method instead
questions.explain: The lesson's core warning: informal identification misses people whose late objections are the costliest to discover.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say contested, one-off decisions need something beyond the RACI matrix?
options: RACI is built for recurring activities, while contested decisions need sharper, pre-agreed clarity on who has final say
RACI only applies to IT departments, not governance
RACI already fully solves one-off contested decisions with no gaps
Decision rights frameworks replace the need for a RACI matrix entirely
questions.explain: The lesson distinguishes RACI's fit for recurring activities from decision-rights frameworks' fit for one-off, contested decisions.

questions.q: Which of these is one of the seven sections of the reusable policy document template?
options: Owner and approver, tied to the RACI matrix
A list of software license costs
The personal phone numbers of committee members
A full technical implementation guide for developers
questions.explain: Owner/approver is one of the seven template sections; implementation detail belongs in a standard, not the policy.

questions.q: What is the key difference the lesson draws between a procedure and a workflow?
options: A procedure answers what one person does for one task; a workflow answers what happens as a request moves across different roles
There is no real difference between a procedure and a workflow
A workflow only applies to IT systems, while a procedure applies to policy
A procedure is always longer and more detailed than a workflow
questions.explain: The lesson distinguishes single-person step-by-step instructions (procedure) from a multi-role, end-to-end path (workflow).

questions.q: Which of these is an example of a "working," checkable standard rather than a weak one?
options: "Customer PII fields must be encrypted at rest using AES-256 or stronger"
"Customer data should be reasonably protected"
"We care deeply about customer privacy"
"Data should generally be kept secure"
questions.explain: A checkable standard names a specific, verifiable rule that can be answered yes or no — the vaguer options can't be.

questions.q: Which is listed as an example adoption metric in this lesson?
options: Percentage of new reports or dashboards built against approved, governed data sources
Server uptime percentage
Number of office locations
Total company revenue
questions.explain: The lesson lists governed-source usage, steward engagement, and glossary usage as adoption metrics — not infrastructure or financial metrics.

questions.q: The lesson gives "number of policies published" as an example of what?
options: A vanity metric — it looks good but doesn't drive any decision
A strong leading indicator
A required program-health KPI
An adoption metric
questions.explain: It goes up regardless of whether anyone follows the policies, so it fails the lesson's test: would anyone change what they do if it moved?

questions.q: What does the lesson say about Power BI's Goals feature in relation to data governance?
options: It wasn't built for governance specifically, but its current value / target / trend / status structure fits a governance program's needs
It was built specifically as a data governance product
It cannot track more than one metric at a time
It replaces the need for KPIs entirely
questions.explain: The lesson is explicit that Goals is a general-purpose feature, used here as an example of the right structure, not a governance-specific tool.

questions.q: The lesson warns that a program hitting every metric target can still be failing. Why?
options: The targets may have been set too low to matter, or a team may have learned to game the metric instead of improving the real behavior
Metric targets are always set correctly, so this can't actually happen
Hitting every target always means true success
Dashboards are incapable of showing all-green status
questions.explain: The lesson gives these two specific failure modes: targets set too low, and metrics being gamed rather than the underlying behavior improving.

questions.q: According to the lesson, what's the risk of escalating resistance too early?
options: It burns trust and teaches people that raising concerns gets them labeled as a blocker
There is no risk to escalating early
Early escalation always resolves the issue instantly
It automatically triggers a policy rewrite
questions.explain: The lesson warns that escalating before genuinely trying to understand the resistance discourages people from raising legitimate concerns in the future.

questions.q: According to the lesson's tailoring table, what should a message to the 'low influence, high impact' group emphasize?
options: Exactly what changes in their daily workflow, with concrete before/after examples
The company's overall business case and financial risk
Nothing — this group needs no communication at all
A request for a public endorsement
questions.explain: The lesson's table specifically assigns practical workflow detail to the low-influence, high-impact quadrant, not business-case framing.

questions.q: Where does the lesson say most governance programs get stuck?
options: Between "aware but resistant" and "compliant" — people do the minimum because it's mandatory, not because they've bought in
They never progress past "unaware"
They skip straight to "engaged" without any resistance
They oscillate randomly between all four stages
questions.explain: The lesson specifically says most programs stall between resistant and compliant, producing fragile, enforcement-dependent behavior.

questions.q: How does the lesson distinguish process training from data literacy?
options: Process training is narrow and tied to one specific tool or workflow; data literacy is broader, more durable understanding that makes future process training land faster
They are two names for the exact same activity
Data literacy is only for executives, and process training is only for analysts
Process training never goes stale, while data literacy expires every quarter
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly separates narrow, tool-specific process training from broader, durable data literacy.

questions.q: How does the roadmap's now/next/later structure (Lesson 21) help when a budget gets cut, per this lesson?
options: It lets the program name precisely what stays, what slips, and what waits, instead of the whole program collapsing
It has no relationship to budget conversations at all
It guarantees the budget can never be cut
It requires canceling every committed 'Now' item automatically
questions.explain: Because the backlog is already sorted by horizon and priority, a cut can be absorbed precisely rather than catastrophically.

questions.q: How does this lesson distinguish a maturity assessment from the KPI dashboards covered in Chapter 3?
options: A dashboard tracks ongoing operational health month to month; a maturity assessment asks a slower-moving question about structural capability over time
They are exactly the same thing with different names
A maturity assessment replaces the need for any KPIs at all
Dashboards are only used once, at program launch
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly frames the dashboard as the operational view and the maturity assessment as the slower, structural-capability view.

questions.q: Why are 'Later' items described loosely on purpose?
options: So the roadmap doesn't pretend to know things it doesn't know yet that far out
Because the program has already decided to cancel them
Because loose descriptions are faster to write and that's the only reason
Because 'Later' items are never real candidates, just filler
questions.explain: Later items are real candidates, but describing them loosely keeps the roadmap honest about the limits of what can be firmly planned far in advance.

questions.q: Why did Brightfield's adoption effort nearly stall, per this lesson's application of Chapter 4?
options: Field agronomists saw the new workflow as added friction to their fieldwork, with no new policy fixing that by itself
The governance council wrote no policy at all
There were no KPIs or dashboards of any kind
The company had no governance charter
questions.explain: The problem was adoption among people doing daily field work, not a gap in policy, measurement, or charter — which is why the fix was communication and peer-led training, not a new rule.
